title: Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu opening

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu defined the highest bhakti: turning to Krishna gladly, with nothing laid over the love. Today, one line in it that looks like a typo.

Some players reach the final boss of a game they love and just stop. They wander the map, do side quests, talk to every villager. Beat the boss, and the game ends. Rupa's book has a line like that, and it's strange. Moksha, freedom from the cycle of birth and death, is the far shore some Hindu schools name as the goal past every goal. A few verses into his ocean, Rupa lists what pure bhakti does. And one item on the list says it makes moksha look light. Why would a book of devotion shrug at the finish line?
screen: `THE PLAYER WHO WON'T BEAT THE BOSS.` → `MOKSHA: THE FAR SHORE.` → `WHY SHRUG AT IT?`

segments.voice: Read the whole list, in paraphrase, and the puzzle starts to solve itself. Pure bhakti ends suffering. It brings what is good. It makes liberation seem light. It is very hard to come by. It is a joy that is dense and of a special kind. And it draws Krishna himself. The first marks are what anyone might hope from a spiritual path: less pain, more good. Then the turn. Then the reason for the turn. This joy is thick, concentrated, and it pulls on Krishna. A devotee who has tasted it isn't looking for the exit, because the exit was never the prize. The love is. Like the player on the map, the point isn't ending the game. It's being in the world of it, with the one you love. Rupa's view leans on the Bhagavata Purana. In one passage there, Krishna speaks of devotees who won't accept liberation, even when it's offered, if it comes without serving him. And the last mark is the boldest. Bhakti doesn't only carry the devotee toward God. In this lineage, love pulls God toward the devotee. Not every Hindu school weighs it this way. For some, moksha stays the highest aim, and this track will hear one of them next week. Rupa says plainly where his book stands.
screen: `ENDS SUFFERING, BRINGS GOOD.` · `MAKES EVEN LIBERATION LOOK LIGHT.` · `A DENSE AND SPECIAL JOY.` · then, large: `IT DRAWS KRISHNA HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Count, slowly, on your fingers, moments of gladness that didn't ask for anything next: a song in the car, a long laugh, a meal with nobody in a hurry. Stop at three, and stay with whichever one is warmest. If you pray, you can turn that gladness toward Krishna; if not, let the moment be enough.
Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book that lists what pure bhakti does, up to making liberation seem light and drawing Krishna close.

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava teaching, these marks of pure bhakti are read as signs to recognize, and devotees speak of loving service, not liberation, as what they hope for.
